articles.title: Why your feet tell you about heat strain first
articles.deck: Extremities shed heat before core temperature moves. What that means for when you should stop.

sections.text: When your body gets hot, it moves heat to the skin by sending more blood there. The palms and soles are especially good at this. Their hairless (glabrous) skin contains arteriovenous anastomoses: direct shunts between small arteries and veins that can open wide and carry a lot of warm blood close to the surface. That is why your feet can warm noticeably as your body works to shed heat.
In hyperthermia, blood flow to the skin can reach 6 to 8 litres a minute (Charkoudian, 2003).

Thermyx measures foot-contact temperature at the insole, once a second, on each foot. It does not measure core body temperature, and a warm foot on its own does not mean you are overheating: a hot boot, hot ground, or a long walk all warm the foot too. What helps is the pattern. A foot that keeps climbing while the air around you is hot and your steps get less steady is a stronger signal than any one number, which is why Thermyx combines foot temperature, air temperature, and steadiness before it raises the risk level.

When Home shows Caution or higher and your foot temperature is still rising, take a break in the shade, drink water, and switch the insoles to Cool. Check again in ten minutes: the trend should level off or fall.

articles.sources: Sources: Charkoudian N. Skin blood flow in adult human thermoregulation: how it works, when it does not, and why. Mayo Clinic Proceedings. 2003;78(5):603–612. doi:10.4065/78.5.603.

articles.title: How Thermyx heats and cools
articles.deck: One thin tile does both jobs. Here's how a Peltier module moves heat, and why the fan runs with it.

sections.text: Thermyx heats and cools with a Peltier module: a thin ceramic tile packed with tiny blocks of two kinds of semiconductor. When current flows through it, heat is carried from one face to the other, so one face gets colder and the other hotter. This is the Peltier effect, described by Jean Peltier in 1834. There are no moving parts and no refrigerant.

Reverse the current and the faces swap. That is how one module does both jobs: current one way warms the side against your foot, the other way cools it. The heat has to go somewhere, though. When the insole cools your foot, the far face gets hot, and that heat, plus the module's own waste heat, has to be carried away or the cool side warms back up.

That is the fan's job, so Thermyx runs the fan whenever it is heating or cooling. A Peltier module also uses a lot of power for the heat it moves, which is why Auto idles whenever your foot is already in range.
If cooling feels weak, check that nothing is covering the fan vent and that the battery isn't low. Use Auto for long wear: it saves battery by only running the module when it's needed.

articles.sources: Sources: the Peltier effect is standard thermoelectric physics. How the fan and Auto behave comes from the Thermyx prototype.

articles.title: What each mode does
articles.deck: Cool, Auto, Heat and Off, and the safety limits that apply to each.

sections.text: Cool runs the module to draw heat away from your foot for as long as it's selected. Heat runs it the other way to warm your foot. Heat has two safety limits: the insole stops heating if the contact temperature reaches 40 °C (104 °F) and only resumes below 38.5 °C (101.3 °F), and the app locks Heat out and switches to Cool if your risk level reaches High or Critical.

Auto holds your target temperature. Calibration sets it from what you said felt comfortable, and you can change it in Profile, Advanced, between 26 and 38 °C. Below the target Auto heats, above it Auto cools, and close to it Auto idles, with a small margin so it doesn't flick on and off at the edge.
Off turns the module and the fan off. The insole keeps sensing, so readings, insights and safety alerts still work.
Most of the time, Auto is the one to use. Pick Cool or Heat for a quick change, and Off to save battery when you don't need either.

articles.sources: Sources: the limits and ranges are the ones set in the Thermyx app and firmware.

articles.title: Reading your comfort band
articles.deck: What the shaded range on your temperature chart means, and what falling outside it does and does not tell you.

sections.text: The shaded range on your temperature charts is the comfort band: 30–34 °C (86–93 °F) of foot-contact temperature. Readings are coloured by where they fall: below 30 °C is Cool, 30–34 °C is Comfort, 34–37 °C is Warm, and 37 °C and above is Hot. The heat-exposure ring on Insights shows how much of your wear time was spent above the band.

The band is a fixed range chosen for the prototype, not a personal baseline and not a medical threshold. Feet vary: yours may sit warm or cool for perfectly ordinary reasons like your socks, your shoes, or the ground. Time above the band tells you your feet spent time warm. It does not tell you that you are ill, and time inside it does not prove you are safe. The risk level on Home, which also looks at air temperature and steadiness, is the better guide in the moment.

The first time you see a long stretch above the band, look at what you were doing then: the air temperature, your shoes, and whether you were resting or working. If the risk level was also raised, plan more shade and water breaks for that kind of day.

articles.sources: Sources: the band edges are set in the app (ThermyxTemperatureScale). No outside claim is made about what the band means for health.

articles.title: Cold feet, poor circulation, and warming safely
articles.deck: Warming a cold foot too fast carries its own risks. How to use the heating mode without creating a burn.

sections.text: Cold feet need warming gently. Numb or very cold skin cannot feel heat properly, so it is easy to burn it with a heat source that would feel fine on warm skin. Frostbite guidance from the Wilderness Medical Society says to avoid heat sources such as fires and space heaters because of the risk of burns, and to rewarm in water held at 37–39 °C (98.6–102.2 °F) with a thermometer when rewarming is needed. If a foot is white, waxy, hard, or has lost feeling, that is a medical problem: get care rather than warming it with the insole.

Some people should talk to a clinician before using any heat on their feet, including anyone with diabetes, peripheral neuropathy, or poor circulation, because they may not feel a burn happening. Thermyx limits heating in two places: the app turns heating off and raises the risk level if foot contact reaches 40 °C, and the insole firmware refuses to heat at that limit on its own.

Use Auto with a modest target (30–32 °C) rather than Heat when your feet are cold, and check your feet after the first 20 minutes. Stop heating if your feet feel numb, tingle strongly, or look red or blistered.

articles.sources: Sources: McIntosh SE, et al. Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Frostbite: 2024 Update. Wilderness & Environmental Medicine. 2024;35(2):183–197. doi:10.1177/10806032231222359.

articles.title: Fatigue shows up in your gait before you feel it
articles.deck: Stability, cadence, and load shift as a shift wears on. What Thermyx can and cannot read from that.

sections.text: As muscles tire, walking changes, but not always in the same way. A 2019 systematic review of fatigue experiments in healthy older adults found small changes in step length, step width, and walking speed, and more variable trunk movement, with results that differed between studies and test setups. Thermyx watches three related things from the insole: steadiness (how regular your step timing is), cadence (steps per minute), and how much of your weight goes through the front of your foot. With two insoles it can also see when you start favouring one side.

These are clues, not a diagnosis. Steadiness changes with the ground, your shoes, carrying a load, or simply slowing down. Thermyx does not predict falls; that is a research question, not something this app claims to do. A drop in steadiness raises the risk level only as one signal among several.

If Home shows your steadiness below your usual level, slow down and take a break. If you are also hot, treat it as a heat warning: shade, water, and Cool. If one foot keeps taking more load, check your shoes and anything that hurts.

articles.sources: Sources: Effects of experimentally induced fatigue on healthy older adults' gait: a systematic review. PLOS ONE. 2019;14(12):e0226939. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0226939.

articles.title: Hydration, shade, and the 20-minute rule
articles.deck: The countermeasures that actually move the needle when a warning fires.

sections.text: Occupational heat guidance comes down to three things: water, rest, and shade. NIOSH recommends drinking 1 cup (8 oz) of water every 15–20 minutes when working in the heat, and warns against drinking more than 48 oz (1½ quarts) an hour. Regular rest in a cool or shaded area matters too, and so does building up gradually: OSHA reports that almost half of heat-related deaths at work happen on a worker's first day, and over 70 percent in the first week. OSHA's heat campaign uses the same three words: Water. Rest. Shade.
1 cup of water every 15–20 minutes when working in the heat, and no more than 48 oz an hour (NIOSH).
Thermyx's cooling can make your feet more comfortable, but it does not cool your whole body and does not replace these steps.
When a warning fires: stop, get into shade, drink a cup of water, and switch the insoles to Cool. Rest until the risk level drops, then keep drinking a cup every 15–20 minutes.

articles.sources: Sources: NIOSH. Heat Stress: Hydration (DHHS/NIOSH Publication 2017-126). OSHA. Heat — Protecting New Workers (osha.gov/heat-exposure/protecting-new-workers).

articles.title: What Thermyx is not
articles.deck: An investigational warning aid, not a diagnosis. The limits, stated plainly.

sections.text: Thermyx is an investigational heat-risk warning aid. It does not measure core body temperature, it does not diagnose heat illness or any other condition, and it is not a medical device or a substitute for medical care. It can be wrong, it can lose connection, and it can miss things.

Call 911 for anyone who shows signs of heat stroke, whatever the app shows: confusion or slurred speech, loss of consciousness, seizures, hot red skin that is dry or damp, or a very high body temperature (103 °F / 39.4 °C or higher). Heat stroke is a medical emergency. While you wait, move them somewhere cooler and cool them with cold water, ice, or cool cloths. Heat exhaustion (heavy sweating, cold and clammy skin, nausea or vomiting, dizziness, headache, cramps, fatigue) means stop, move somewhere cool, loosen clothing, and sip water; get medical help if they are vomiting, if it gets worse, or if it lasts longer than an hour (CDC; OSHA).
Trust how you and the people around you feel over what the app says. If someone is confused, faints, or has a seizure in the heat, call 911 first and look at the app later.

articles.sources: Sources: CDC. Warning Signs and Symptoms of Heat-Related Illness (cdc.gov/disasters/extremeheat). OSHA. Heat-Related Illnesses and First Aid (osha.gov/heat-exposure/illness-first-aid).

articles.title: How to read your insights
articles.deck: What the daily summary, the shaded temperature chart, and the activity split are telling you.

sections.text: The cards at the top of Insights are today's summary: how long you wore Thermyx, how long it heated and cooled, and your average foot temperature. Tap one to open that day's page, or open Daily summaries for earlier days. A week of summaries tells you more than any single reading.

On the temperature chart, the line is your foot-contact temperature. Red shading behind it marks when the insole was heating, and blue when it was cooling. The band shows the comfort range. If the line keeps climbing while the shading is blue, the insole is working hard to keep up, which is worth noticing on a hot day.
Activity splits your wear time into sitting, standing and walking, and estimates your steps from cadence. These are estimates from pressure and movement, not a medical measurement.
Check your summary at the end of the day for a week. Look for patterns: which days ran hot, when you relied on cooling, and whether your walking time changed.
